title: What coding interviews look like, and thinking out loud
summary: The rounds of an AI engineer interview loop, what the interviewer is really scoring, and a six-step routine for talking through any problem.
youWillLearn: The usual rounds in an AI engineer interview loop, and which ones this module prepares you for
What the interviewer writes on the scorecard: the process, not only the answer
A six-step routine for any problem: clarify, examples, brute force, code, test, improve
How to get unstuck out loud, and how to practice with Claude without letting it solve for you

glossary.interview loop: The full set of interviews for one job, often spread over a day or a week, each round testing a different skill.
glossary.live coding: A round where you solve a small programming problem in a shared editor while the interviewer watches and talks with you.
glossary.take-home: A small project you build on your own time and hand in, usually followed by a call where you walk through it.
glossary.scorecard: The form an interviewer fills in after the round, rating skills like communication, problem solving and code quality.
glossary.brute force: The simplest solution that is clearly correct, even if it is slow. You find it first, then improve it.
glossary.edge case: An unusual input that often breaks code: an empty list, one item, duplicates, negative numbers, huge input.
glossary.constraints: The limits of the problem: how big the input can be, what values are allowed, how fast the answer must be.
glossary.shared editor: A web page where you and the interviewer see and edit the same code at the same time.

steps.title: You, an interviewer and a shared editor
body: You built Notely, a notes app with an AI Summarize button, using Claude Code. Now you are applying for AI engineer jobs.
Most hiring processes include a live coding round: you solve a small problem in a shared editor, a web page where you both see the same code. An interviewer watches, talks and takes notes.

scene.caption: You type into the shared editor. The interviewer watches the same screen.

steps.title: Twenty silent minutes is a failing grade
body: You read the problem, go quiet, and type for twenty minutes. The code even works.
You still get a no. The interviewer saw nothing of how you got there, so they had nothing to write down. A live coding round grades your thinking, and silent thinking is invisible.

callout.text: A design crit where you show only the final screen. No problem framing, no rejected options, no reasons. Even a good screen gets a weak review, because nobody can judge your judgment.

changes: ~ Silent minutes 0 → 20
~ Scorecard notes stay at 0: nothing to write down
~ You and Interviewer: both uneasy

scene.caption: Lots of typing, no talking. The interviewer has nothing to grade.

steps.title: They grade the process, not only the answer
body: After the round, the interviewer fills in a scorecard: a form that rates how you communicate, how you break the problem down, how clean your code is, and how you test it.
A correct answer covers only part of that. Saying your thinking out loud fills in the rest, and lets the interviewer give you hints.
changes: + Scorecard: the form the interviewer fills in after
+ A line from You to Interviewer: you think out loud
~ Silent minutes 20 → 0
~ Scorecard notes 0 → 4, one per skill

scene.caption: Thinking out loud turns invisible work into notes on the scorecard.

steps.title: The rounds of an AI engineer loop
body: An interview loop is every round for one job. It often mixes a recruiter call, live coding or a take-home project, system design, a practical AI build (call a model, handle its answer) and a behavioral talk about past work.
Formats vary. Ask the recruiter which rounds you will get, and whether AI tools are allowed in each.

callout.text: Your system design course covers that round. This module covers the coding round: the data structures and patterns interviewers still expect you to reason about without help.

changes: − You, Shared editor, Interviewer, Scorecard: we step back
+ Recruiter call, Live coding, Take-home: the early rounds
+ System design, AI build, Behavioral: the later rounds

scene.caption: A typical loop. This module prepares you for the coding round.

steps.title: One routine for every problem
body: In the coding round, use the same six moves every time, and say each one out loud: clarify the problem, walk through examples, state a brute force idea (slow but surely correct), code it, test it by hand, then improve it.
A fixed routine keeps you calm. When your mind goes blank, you still know the next move.
changes: − Recruiter call, Live coding, Take-home
− System design, AI build, Behavioral: we zoom into coding
+ Clarify, Examples, Brute force: the first three moves
+ Code, Test, Improve: the last three moves

scene.caption: Six moves in a loop. Each one is a sentence you say out loud.

steps.title: Clarify before you type a line
body: Problems are left vague on purpose. Asking good questions is part of the test, exactly like a client brief.
Ask about the constraints (how big can the input get?) and the edge cases (empty input, duplicates, ties). Then write your assumptions as a comment at the top, so you both see them.

code.caption: Assumptions written down are assumptions the interviewer can correct early.

changes: ~ Clarify: in focus, with three questions to ask
~ The other five moves fade for now

scene.caption: Clarifying comes first. It is the cheapest place to catch a misunderstanding.

steps.title: What thinking out loud sounds like
body: Narrate decisions, not keystrokes. Say what you are about to do and why, then do it.

For example: "My first idea: for each tag, count how often it appears in the whole list. Slow, since it rescans the list every time, but surely correct. Let me check with ['ai', 'work', 'ai']: I expect 'ai'."

callout.text: Useful phrases: "My first idea is…", "The cost of that is…", "I'm assuming…, is that okay?", "Let me trace a small example." Each one gives the interviewer something to write down.

changes: ~ Clarify: done
~ Examples: done, with one list of three tags
~ Brute force: in focus, said out loud

scene.caption: Questions, then a small example, then a first idea: each move said out loud.

steps.title: Stuck? Say so, then shrink the problem
body: The classic mistake is to freeze, or to fake progress by typing random code. Both look worse than an honest "I'm stuck".

Say what you know, then solve a tiny version by hand: two items, then three. Patterns show up in small examples. If the interviewer offers a hint, take it. Using a hint well scores better than refusing it.

callout.text: Do not stay silent for more than a minute or so. Even "I'm considering a map here, give me a moment to check it works" keeps the interviewer with you.

changes: ~ Brute force: done
~ Code: stuck
~ Examples: back to a tiny one, 2 items
+ A dashed line from Code back to Examples

scene.caption: Stuck while coding? Go back to a tiny example, out loud.

steps.title: Practice with Claude as the interviewer
body: You already work with Claude. For practice, flip its role: ask it to play the interviewer, not to solve the problem.

Paste a problem, type out your plan, and let it question you. Some companies now allow AI tools in certain rounds. There, they grade how well you guide and check the AI, so the same reasoning skills apply.

callout.text: Set the rules first: no code from Claude, questions back, one small hint only when you ask, and a score at the end. If it starts writing the solution, stop it and restate the rules.

code.code:
You are my interviewer for a 45-minute coding round.
Problem: return the most used tag in a list of tags.
Rules: no code from you. Ask about my plan and its cost.
Hint only if I type HINT. At the end, grade me on:
communication, problem solving, code, testing.
code.caption: Save this as a snippet and reuse it with every practice problem.

changes: − Clarify, Examples, Brute force, Code, Test, Improve
+ You: practicing at home
+ Claude: plays the interviewer and asks questions back
+ Scorecard: Claude's feedback at the end

scene.caption: In practice, Claude asks the questions. You do the thinking.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: A coding round grades your process. Run the same six moves every time: clarify, examples, brute force, code, test, improve, and say each one out loud.
Stuck is normal: say so and shrink the problem. Practice with Claude as the interviewer, never as the answer key.
changes: ~ You and Scorecard turn green: the routine works

scene.caption: Your thinking, said out loud, is what ends up on the scorecard.

quiz.question: You are given "find duplicate notes" in a live round. What is the best first thing to say?

options.text: "I'll loop once and remember what I've seen." Then start typing.
options.why: The idea may be right, but you skipped clarifying. What counts as a duplicate: same title, same body, ignoring case? You might solve the wrong problem fast.

options.text: "Does duplicate mean the same title or the same content, and should case matter?"
options.why: Clarifying first catches misunderstandings when they are cheapest, and it shows the interviewer you treat problems like real briefs.

options.text: Nothing yet. Think quietly until you have the full solution.
options.why: Silent thinking is invisible on the scorecard, and it stops the interviewer from steering you with hints.

quiz.question: Halfway through, you realize your approach does not handle ties. What do you do?

options.text: Say it out loud, explain the gap, and decide with the interviewer how ties should work.
options.why: Finding your own bug and handling it calmly is exactly what the testing and communication parts of the scorecard reward.

options.text: Keep going and hope the interviewer does not notice.
options.why: They usually notice, and hiding it scores worse than fixing it openly.

options.text: Delete everything and start over with a new idea.
options.why: Ties are a small change to a working approach. Throwing everything away wastes time you need for testing.

quiz.question: You want to use Claude Code to prepare. Which setup actually builds interview skill?

options.text: Ask Claude for the optimal solution to 100 problems and read them all.
options.why: Reading answers feels productive but trains recognition, not the out-loud problem solving the round tests.

options.text: Have Claude solve each problem, then copy its code by hand.
options.why: Copying builds typing speed, not reasoning. You never practice getting unstuck.

options.text: Have Claude play the interviewer: no code, questions back, hints only on request, a score at the end.
options.why: This rehearses the real round: you think, explain and test, and you get feedback on the same skills the scorecard rates.

takeaways: Coding rounds grade the process: communication, problem solving, code and testing. Silent thinking scores nothing.
Run the same six moves every time: clarify, examples, brute force, code, test, improve.
Write your assumptions as a comment at the top of the editor so the interviewer can correct them early.
Stuck? Say so, then solve a tiny version by hand. Taking a hint well is a good signal.
Ask the recruiter which rounds you will get and whether AI tools are allowed in each.
